unit.title: Establish and maintain a strategic planning cycle

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a strategic planning cycle in a public body?
options: To link direction, plans, budgets and results, and review them
To produce one plan every ten years and then leave it unchanged
To replace the annual budget with a list of the Minister's ideas
To give each division its own goals, unrelated to the others

questions.stem: Which order best shows the main stages of a strategic planning cycle?
options: Implement, budget, analyse, review, set direction
Review, implement, set direction, plan, analyse
Analyse, set direction, plan, implement, review
Set direction, implement, analyse, plan, review

questions.stem: A ministry's draft strategic plan makes no link to the national development plan. Why is this a problem?
options: National plans apply only to private businesses
Its work may not support agreed national priorities
The draft will be too short to be approved
Ministries are not allowed their own plans

questions.stem: Why should a ministry's planning calendar be set to match the Government's budget cycle?
options: So that plans can be written after the budget is spent
So the planning unit can take leave during budget time
So that divisions need not submit budgets for their plans
So that plans are ready in time to shape budget bids

questions.stem: On what date does the Government of Jamaica's financial year begin?
options: 1 January
1 July
1 April
1 October

questions.stem: A planning team at an agency studies changes in technology, the economy, the law and the population that may affect its work. What is this called?
options: An environmental scan
A staff performance appraisal
A bank reconciliation
A stock take

questions.stem: In a SWOT analysis for a public agency, which item is a weakness?
options: A new government policy that increases the agency's funding
An outdated case system that slows service to the public
Rising public demand for online services across the island
A partner agency offering to share its training rooms

questions.stem: Which statement is a mission rather than a vision?
options: A Jamaica where every child reads well by age eight
To be the Caribbean's leading water utility by 2035
A healthy, safe and prosperous parish for all residents
We provide safe, reliable water to homes and businesses

questions.stem: Why should a ministry consult staff, partner agencies and the public when it sets its strategic priorities?
options: Their views improve the plan and build support for it
Consultation means the senior team need not decide anything
The law requires every citizen to approve each ministry's plan
It allows the ministry to put off the plan for another year

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a strategic plan and an operational plan?
options: Strategic lists daily tasks; operational sets the long-term vision
Strategic covers one month; operational covers ten years or more
Strategic sets direction; operational sets the year's work
Strategic is written by staff; operational only by the Minister

questions.stem: In a results chain, what comes between activities and outcomes?
options: Inputs
Impact
Baselines
Outputs

questions.stem: A ministry trains 500 farmers in new irrigation methods. Which of these is an outcome rather than an output?
options: 500 farmers attended the training sessions
Crop yields of trained farmers rose by 20%
20 training sessions were held in four parishes
1,000 training manuals were printed and handed out

questions.stem: Before setting a target to cut the time taken to issue permits, what should the planning team find out first?
options: How long other countries' ministers have been in office
How many permits the agency issued twenty years ago
The current average time taken, as a baseline
Which officers would like to join the permit team

questions.stem: A target is to raise the share of births registered within 30 days from a baseline of 60% to 80%. The latest figure is 72%. What share of the planned improvement has been achieved?
Which is the best key performance indicator for a goal to improve customer service at a tax office?
options: Number of computers bought this year
Share of customers served within 20 minutes
Number of staff meetings held each quarter
Number of pages in the office's annual report

questions.stem: A ministry has more proposed projects than its budget can fund. What is the best basis for choosing which ones go into the plan?
options: The projects put forward by the most senior directors
The projects that were in last year's plan, unchanged
The cheapest projects, whatever they would achieve
Agreed criteria, such as fit with goals, impact and cost

questions.stem: Project A scores 8 for impact (60% weight) and 5 for cost (40% weight). Project B scores 6 for impact and 9 for cost. Which has the higher weighted score?
options: Project A, with 6.8
Both score 7.0
Project B, with 7.2
Project A, with 7.4

questions.stem: During the budget process, a division asks for money for a project that is not in the strategic plan. What should the planning unit advise?
options: Show how it fits the plan, or put it through a review
Fund it at once, since budgets matter more than plans do
Fund it quietly and leave it out of the progress reports
Cut another division's projects to make room for it

questions.stem: How should a ministry's strategic objectives reach individual officers?
options: Through a copy of the plan emailed once to all staff
Only through the Minister's speeches in Parliament
They need not reach officers, only senior managers
Through division plans, unit plans and work plans

questions.stem: What is the main role of a ministry's corporate planning unit in the planning cycle?
options: To set the ministry's policy priorities in place of the Minister
To coordinate the process, set the calendar and compile reports
To write every division's plan without asking the divisions
To approve all of the spending by the ministry's divisions

questions.stem: What is the role of the senior executive team in the strategic planning cycle?
options: To leave planning entirely to the planning unit
To sign the plan without reading or discussing it
To set direction, agree priorities and own the plan
To write the detailed work plan for every officer

questions.stem: How often should a ministry's management team usually review progress on its operational plan?
options: Each quarter, with a fuller mid-year review
Only once the whole three-year plan has come to an end
Only when the Auditor General asks to see the plan
Every day, with a full rewrite of the plan each time

questions.stem: A quarterly report shows that a key project is three months behind schedule. What should the planning unit do?
options: Leave the project out of the report so results look better
Wait for the annual review before raising the matter
Change the target so that the project appears on track
Flag it, find the cause and agree action with the owner

questions.stem: What is a "rolling" strategic plan?
options: A plan written once and kept unchanged until it ends
A plan updated each year, adding a new year at the end
A plan that moves from one ministry to another each year
A plan with no targets, so that it can change at any time

questions.stem: A major hurricane damages roads and schools in three parishes in the middle of the plan period. What should the ministry do with its strategic plan?
options: Review priorities and update the plan and budget as needed
Carry on exactly as planned, since the plan is approved
Stop all planning until after the next general election
Wait until the plan period ends to record the hurricane

questions.stem: Why might a planning team use scenario planning?
options: To predict the exact future so that no review is needed
To decide which officers will be promoted in future years
To test how the strategy holds up under different futures
To remove the need for any targets in the plan

questions.stem: Where should a ministry record the main risks to achieving its strategic objectives?
options: In the minutes of the staff social committee
In a strategic risk register linked to the plan
In each officer's personal diary
In the visitors' book at the front desk

questions.stem: Which question about resources should a planning team answer before finalising its plan?
options: Which offices have the best view of the sea?
Which divisions held the most social events last year?
How many new cars do the senior managers want?
Do we have the money, staff and skills to deliver it?

questions.stem: After a new strategic plan is approved, what is the best way to communicate it to staff?
options: Store it on the shared drive and say no more about it
Give copies only to directors, to keep in their offices
Hold briefings, share a summary and link it to unit plans
Read the full plan aloud at one meeting for all staff

questions.stem: At the end of a three-year plan, what is the main purpose of evaluating it?
options: To judge what was achieved and why, to inform the next plan
To find the officers to blame for any targets that were missed
To close the plan's files and start a new plan from nothing
To prove that every target in the plan was fully met

questions.stem: How does a public body's annual report fit into the strategic planning cycle?
options: It replaces the need for an operational plan for the year
It reports results against the plan to the public
It sets the vision and mission for the next ten years
It is written before the plan to guess what will happen

questions.stem: Divisions report their key performance figures in different ways, so the totals cannot be compared. What should the planning unit do?
options: Accept the figures and add them up anyway
Choose the most favourable figure from each division
Stop reporting the indicators until the next plan
Agree definitions and data sources for each indicator

questions.stem: How can a ministry make sure staff appraisals support the strategic plan?
options: Link officers' work plan targets to the plan
Base appraisals only on attendance and punctuality records
Give every officer the same rating to keep things fair
Keep appraisals and plans completely separate from each other

questions.stem: Why should a public body write down its planning procedures, calendar and templates?
options: So only the planning unit understands how the cycle works
So that the process can change completely every year
So the cycle runs the same way even as staff change
So that divisions can skip any steps they find inconvenient

questions.stem: An agency's annual target is 1,200 inspections. By the end of September, six months into the financial year, it has done 540. What percentage of the annual target is that?
Halfway through the financial year, an agency has completed 45% of its annual target for inspections. What should management conclude?
options: The agency has already failed and the target should be dropped
The agency is well ahead and can now reduce its effort
Nothing yet, since only the year-end result matters
It is a little behind and should check whether it can catch up

questions.stem: A ministry's budget of J$2,400,000,000 is shared among its three strategic goals in the ratio 3:2:1. How much goes to the first goal?
A ministry's draft plan lists 28 "top priority" goals. What is the main problem?
options: Too many priorities spread effort and money too thinly
The law says a plan must have exactly ten goals
Twenty-eight goals would all be too easy to reach
The planning unit would run out of printing paper

questions.stem: Why are core values, such as integrity and respect, included in a strategic plan?
options: They replace the need for any measurable targets
They are needed only for the annual report's cover
They tell staff which projects to fund first
They guide how staff behave in carrying it out

questions.stem: A planning team plots stakeholders by power and interest. A key donor has high power but little interest in day-to-day work. How should the team manage this donor?
options: Ignore it until the plan is completely finished
Keep it satisfied with regular, targeted updates
Invite it to every weekly planning meeting
Send it the full monthly data files, unexplained

questions.stem: What is the best way to make sure lessons from one planning cycle improve the next?
options: Start each new plan from a completely blank page
Keep the lessons in the minds of senior staff only
Record lessons and review them as the next cycle begins
Note lessons only in years when targets were missed

questions.stem: In a statutory body with a board of directors, who normally approves the strategic plan?
options: The board, after the executive team has prepared it
The most junior officers in each of the divisions
The body's external auditors, at year end
The suppliers who provide the body's main services

questions.stem: Which is NOT normally a stage of a strategic planning cycle?
options: Analysing the environment
Setting goals and priorities
Monitoring and reviewing results
Signing off petty cash vouchers

questions.stem: Over what period does a public body's strategic plan usually look ahead?
options: One month
Three to five years
Twenty-five years or more
One week

questions.stem: Why is strategic planning described as a "cycle" rather than a one-off event?
options: Results feed back into the next round of planning
The same plan is copied out again every year
Planning staff move between ministries each year
Plans must be printed on a round template each year

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Which four-letter tool sets a public body's internal strengths and weaknesses beside its external opportunities and threats?
What is the name of Jamaica's long-term national development plan, which ministries' plans should support?
In a results chain, what word describes the long-term change in society that a programme contributes to, beyond its outcomes?
What is the name of the yearly plan that sets out a division's activities, targets and budget for the year?
What word names the forward-looking statement of what an organisation wants to become or achieve in the long term?
A target is to cut the average processing time from 30 days to 21 days. What percentage reduction is this?
An operational plan has 40 activities for the year. By year end, 34 are complete. What percentage of the activities is complete?
A ministry's capital budget is J$900,000,000, and 15% is set aside for its digital services goal. How much is that? Give the answer in J$.
What term describes the review held halfway through the financial year to check progress on the operational plan?
What is the name of the table that lists each objective with its indicators, baselines, targets and data sources?
What name is given to the document that sets out each ministry's planned spending for the financial year and is laid before Parliament?
What two-word term describes the schedule that sets the dates for each step of the planning and reporting cycle?
What word is used for the gap between planned and actual results or spending?
What word names a measurable statement of the level of performance to be reached by a set date?
What word describes an organisation's ability, in staff, skills, systems and money, to deliver its plan?

essays.stem: A new government agency has been set up with no planning system. As head of its planning unit, explain how you would establish a strategic planning cycle.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by getting the support of the chief executive and the board, and agreeing that the agency needs a three-to-four-year strategic plan and annual operational plans linked to the budget. I would map the stages of the cycle: environmental analysis, setting direction, objectives and targets, operational planning and budgeting, implementation, monitoring, evaluation and review. Next I would draw up a planning calendar fitted to the financial year that runs from April to March, so that plans are ready before budget submissions are due, with dates for quarterly reports, a mid-year review and an annual review. I would set out clear roles: the board approves, the executive team sets direction and owns the plan, the planning unit coordinates and reports, and division heads prepare unit plans and report progress. I would design simple templates for the strategic plan, operational plans and quarterly reports, with a results framework showing indicators, baselines and targets. I would train managers in using them. The procedures would be written down and reviewed after the first cycle, using lessons learned.
markingPoints: Gains leadership support and defines the levels of plan
Maps the stages of the cycle
Sets a planning calendar linked to the April-to-March budget year
Defines roles for the board, executive, planning unit and divisions
Provides templates, a results framework, training and a review of the process

essays.stem: Explain how a parish municipal corporation should analyse its environment at the start of a planning cycle, and how it should use the results to set priorities.
essays.modelAnswer: The corporation should first gather evidence about its external environment using a PESTLE scan: political factors such as new national policies, economic factors such as the local job market and revenue from property taxes, social factors such as population growth and crime, technology such as online payment, legal changes, and environmental issues such as flooding and waste. It should also look inward at its strengths and weaknesses: staff skills, systems, finances, buildings and past performance against targets. Sources would include census data, its own records, the last plan's evaluation, and consultation with councillors, staff, residents, businesses and partner agencies. The findings would be brought together in a SWOT analysis. To set priorities, the planning team would look for strategies that use strengths to take up opportunities and that reduce serious threats or weaknesses, such as poor drainage in flood-prone communities. Possible priorities would be scored against agreed criteria, such as fit with national goals, impact on residents, cost and urgency. The leadership would then choose a small number of priorities and record the evidence behind each choice.
markingPoints: Scans the external environment, e.g. with PESTLE, with local examples
Assesses internal strengths and weaknesses
Uses evidence and consults stakeholders
Brings findings together in a SWOT analysis
Uses agreed criteria to choose a small number of priorities, recording the evidence

essays.stem: A ministry plans a programme to reduce youth unemployment in two parishes. Design a simple results chain for the programme, with an example of an indicator, baseline and target at the outcome level.
essays.modelAnswer: A results chain shows how resources lead to change. The inputs are the money, staff, training centres and partner employers, for example a budget of J$150,000,000 over three years. The activities are recruiting young people, delivering skills courses, arranging work placements and giving job-search support. The outputs are the direct products: for example, 1,500 young people complete a certified course and 900 complete a work placement. The outcomes are the changes for the young people: more of them find and keep jobs. The impact is the long-term change the programme contributes to: lower youth unemployment and less poverty in the two parishes. At outcome level, one indicator could be the percentage of graduates employed six months after finishing. If a survey of an earlier group shows a baseline of 35%, the target might be 60% by the end of year three. The data source would be follow-up phone surveys. I would also note the assumptions, such as employers continuing to hire, and the risks, so the results chain can be tested during monitoring.
markingPoints: Gives suitable inputs and activities
Gives measurable outputs
Distinguishes outcomes from outputs and states the impact
Gives an outcome indicator with a baseline, target and data source
Notes assumptions or risks

essays.stem: Explain why strategic plans and budgets must be linked in a public body, and how a ministry can make sure they are.
essays.modelAnswer: A plan without a budget is a wish list, and a budget without a plan spends money without clear purpose. Linking the two makes sure that public money goes to agreed priorities and that targets are realistic for the resources available. It also helps the ministry explain its spending to the finance ministry, Parliament and the public. To link them, the planning calendar should be set so the strategic priorities and operational plans are agreed before budget submissions are prepared for the financial year starting in April. Each division's budget request should show which strategic objective it supports, and requests for items outside the plan should go through a review. Where money is short, the executive team should use the plan's priorities to decide what to fund, cut or delay, rather than cutting evenly. Once the budget is approved, operational plans and targets should be adjusted to match the money actually allocated. During the year, spending and results should be reported together each quarter, so managers can see what each objective is achieving for its cost.
markingPoints: Explains why plans and budgets must be linked
Sets the planning calendar so plans come before budget bids
Ties each budget request to a strategic objective
Uses plan priorities when money is short and adjusts plans to the final budget
Reports spending and results together during the year

essays.stem: Describe the monitoring and reporting arrangements you would set up to keep an agency's strategic plan on track during the year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make sure each objective in the plan has a small set of indicators with clear definitions, baselines, targets, data sources and a named owner, recorded in a results framework. Division heads would submit a short quarterly report using one template, showing progress on each indicator and activity, spending against budget, reasons for any variance and corrective actions. The planning unit would check the data, ask for evidence where figures look doubtful, and compile a summary dashboard, using a simple traffic-light rating so the executive team can see quickly what is on track, at risk or off track. The executive team would discuss the dashboard each quarter and agree actions for items that are off track. At mid-year, there would be a fuller review, including changes in the environment and the risk register, and the operational plan could be adjusted if needed, with changes recorded. At year end, an annual performance report would be prepared for the board and used in the annual report. Lessons would be noted for the next planning cycle.
markingPoints: Sets indicators with definitions, baselines, targets, sources and owners
Uses a standard quarterly report covering results and spending
Checks data quality and summarises in a dashboard
Holds quarterly executive reviews and a fuller mid-year review with adjustments
Produces an annual report and records lessons

essays.stem: At the end of year two, an agency's three indicators show: permits issued within 10 days, baseline 55%, target 75%, actual 70%; share of services online, baseline 20%, target 50%, actual 26%; customer satisfaction, baseline 68%, target 80%, actual 81%. Analyse the results and recommend actions.
essays.modelAnswer: For permits, the agency planned to improve by 20 percentage points and has improved by 15, so it has achieved 75% of the planned improvement; it is close to target and on a good path. For online services, the planned improvement was 30 points, but it has improved by only 6, or 20% of the planned improvement, so this objective is seriously off track. Customer satisfaction has risen by 13 points against a planned 12, so the target has been exceeded. I would recommend keeping the current approach for permits, with a check on what is holding back the last few points, such as staffing at peak times. For online services, I would investigate the causes: funding delays, weak systems, low staff skills or low public use. Depending on the cause, actions could include re-prioritising budget, a phased plan focused on the most-used services, and public promotion. The target may need to be reset if it was unrealistic, with the reason recorded. For satisfaction, the agency should find out what drove the improvement and keep it going. These findings should feed the mid-term review of the plan.
markingPoints: Calculates progress on permits correctly (15 of 20 points, 75%)
Calculates progress on online services correctly (6 of 30 points, 20%)
Recognises that satisfaction has exceeded its target
Recommends finding causes and specific actions, especially for online services
Considers resetting targets with reasons and feeding the plan review

essays.stem: In the middle of a ministry's three-year plan, its budget is cut by 15% because of a national emergency. Explain how the ministry should review and update its plan.
essays.modelAnswer: The ministry should act quickly but carefully, rather than cutting every programme by 15%. The executive team, supported by the planning unit, should first confirm the size and timing of the cut and any new national priorities linked to the emergency. Next it should review the plan's objectives and programmes against agreed criteria: legal duties that must continue, links to national priorities, impact on the public, especially vulnerable groups, progress so far and cost. This shows which activities to protect, which to scale down or delay and which to stop. The team should look for savings that do not harm results, such as sharing services or delaying non-urgent purchases. Targets must then be revised to match the new resources, and the risk register updated. The revised plan and budget should be approved by the Permanent Secretary and the Minister, or the board where there is one, and the changes explained to staff and stakeholders with reasons. Division and individual work plans should be updated, and the ministry should report progress against the revised targets, keeping a record of what changed and why.
markingPoints: Avoids equal across-the-board cuts and confirms the facts
Reviews programmes against clear criteria, including legal duties and impact
Decides what to protect, reduce, delay or stop, and seeks efficiencies
Revises targets and risks and obtains approval
Communicates the changes and updates lower-level plans and reporting

essays.stem: Explain how you would involve staff and external stakeholders in developing a public body's strategic plan, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Involving people matters because staff and stakeholders hold knowledge the leadership lacks, and because people are more committed to a plan they helped shape. It also builds trust and reduces resistance when the plan is carried out. I would start with a stakeholder analysis to identify who should be involved and how, for example the Minister's office, the board, staff, unions, partner agencies, service users, community groups and donors. For staff, I would run workshops in each division to review the last plan, discuss the environmental analysis and suggest priorities, and use a short anonymous survey so everyone can take part. For external stakeholders, I would hold focus groups or town hall meetings in different parishes, use online surveys, and meet key partners individually. I would make it clear which decisions are open to influence and which are already fixed by policy. The planning team would record all input and show how it was used. Once the plan is drafted, I would share a summary for comment, and after approval I would report back to those who took part, explaining the final choices.
markingPoints: Explains why involvement matters (knowledge, commitment, trust)
Identifies stakeholders through analysis
Uses suitable methods for staff (workshops, surveys)
Uses suitable methods for external stakeholders, clear about what can be influenced
Records input, consults on the draft and reports back

essays.stem: Compare a top-down approach and a participatory (bottom-up) approach to strategic planning in a public body, and recommend the approach you would use.
essays.modelAnswer: In a top-down approach, senior leaders set the vision, objectives and targets and pass them down for divisions to carry out. It is quick, keeps the plan closely aligned with Government policy and gives clear direction. However, it can miss front-line knowledge, set unrealistic targets and leave staff feeling no ownership, which weakens delivery. In a participatory approach, staff at all levels and stakeholders help analyse the situation and propose objectives, and plans are built up from divisions. It uses a wider range of knowledge, produces more realistic targets and builds commitment. However, it takes longer, can produce too many priorities and may drift from national policy if not guided. I would recommend a combined approach. The senior team should set the direction and the key priorities, based on national policy and evidence, and then invite divisions, staff and stakeholders to shape the objectives, targets and actions within that direction. The planning unit would coordinate the process, keep to the calendar and ensure the final plan is focused. This gives clear leadership and real ownership.
markingPoints: Describes the top-down approach with its strengths
Notes the weaknesses of top-down
Describes the participatory approach with strengths and weaknesses
Recommends an approach clearly
Justifies it, explaining how the recommended approach would work

essays.stem: Many strategic plans end up "on the shelf". Explain why this happens and how a manager can keep the strategic planning cycle alive throughout the plan period.
essays.modelAnswer: Plans end up on the shelf when they are written mainly to meet a requirement rather than to guide decisions. Common causes are too many vague priorities, targets with no baselines or owners, no link to the budget, weak communication to staff, and no regular review, so the plan is forgotten once approved. Leaders may also be distracted by daily pressures and crises. To keep the cycle alive, the manager should keep the plan focused on a few clear priorities with measurable targets and named owners. The plan should drive the budget and be cascaded into division, unit and individual work plans, so it shapes daily work and appraisals. Progress should be reported each quarter in a short dashboard and discussed at executive meetings, with action on items off track. A mid-year review and an annual review should test whether the plan still fits the environment and update it when needed. Leaders should refer to the plan when making decisions and communicating with staff. Finally, successes should be celebrated and lessons recorded, so each cycle improves on the last.
markingPoints: Explains why plans are shelved (vague, no owners, no budget link, no review)
Keeps priorities few and targets measurable with owners
Links the plan to budgets and cascades it to work plans
Monitors quarterly and reviews mid-year and annually, updating as needed
Leaders use the plan visibly, celebrate success and record lessons

practical1.title: Design a strategic planning cycle and calendar for a public body
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a new public agency (for example a parish development agency) with its mandate, structure chart and budget dates. As a group, design the agency's strategic planning cycle and the tools to run it. Each member has a named role: process designer (draws the cycle diagram showing each stage and how results feed back into planning); calendar planner (builds a 12-month planning calendar or Gantt chart for the financial year running April to March, showing when the environmental scan, plan approval, budget submission, quarterly reports, mid-year review and annual review happen); roles writer (prepares a table showing who is responsible, who approves, who is consulted and who is informed at each stage: board, executive team, planning unit, division heads and staff); template designer (designs an operational plan template and a quarterly progress report template with indicators, baselines, targets and a traffic-light rating); and presenter (presents the design to the assessor, acting as chief executive, in 10 minutes). In a group of four, the roles writer also presents. Every member must explain their own part during the presentation.
materials: Computers with word processing, spreadsheet and presentation software
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The cycle diagram on the flipchart or screen
The 12-month planning calendar or Gantt chart
The operational plan and quarterly report templates
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
The cycle includes analysis, direction, planning and budgeting, implementation, monitoring, evaluation and review, with feedback
The calendar fits the April-to-March financial year and puts planning before budget submission
Roles are clear, with one approver for each key decision
Templates include indicators, baselines, targets, owners and a status rating
Explained their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Treat the case pack as confidential and return it at the end
Respect each other's ideas and share the workload fairly
Agree the order of tasks early so no member is overloaded near the end
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Run a mid-year review and update an operational plan
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up public body's operational plan with eight indicators (each with a baseline and annual target), the mid-year results, spending against budget in J$, and news of two changes in the environment (for example a budget cut and a new national policy). As a group, carry out a mid-year review and update the plan. Each member has a named role: data analyst (builds a spreadsheet showing, for each indicator, progress against the half-year position, the share of planned improvement achieved and a traffic-light rating, checking every figure twice); environment reviewer (updates the SWOT for the two changes and explains their effect on the plan); risk reviewer (updates the risk register for the objectives most at risk); facilitator (plans and chairs a 25-minute review meeting, with the other members as the executive team, to agree which targets and activities to keep, change or drop); and report writer (writes a two-page mid-year review report with findings, decisions and the revised targets, and a change log). In a group of four, the facilitator also writes the change log. Each decision must be recorded with its reason.
materials: Operational plan, mid-year data and change notices from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processing software
photos: The progress spreadsheet with traffic-light ratings on screen
The updated SWOT on the flipchart
The review meeting in progress, with the agreed decisions on the flipchart (faces only if all agree)
The mid-year review report and the change log
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Progress figures and ratings are correct and were checked twice
The effect of the two changes on the plan is explained clearly
Risks are updated with likelihood, impact, owner and response
Decisions to keep, change or drop targets are reasoned and recorded
The report and change log are clear, accurate and complete
safety: Treat the case data as confidential and return all printouts at the end
Discuss the results of made-up units, not the performance of real people
Keep the review meeting respectful; challenge ideas, not people
Take a short break between the analysis and the meeting
